findings.body: Interpolating owner_id directly into SQL allows its contents to change the WHERE clause rather than remain a customer identifier. findings.failure_scenario: If an attacker can supply owner_id, submitting `' OR 1=1 -- ` makes the query select every customer's orders, exposing data across customer boundaries.

findings.body: The stated intent is a pipeline refactor, but this replaces a weighted-allocation helper with a new database read operation. findings.body: Starting the loop at index 1 excludes entries[0] from the result regardless of its score. This loses an invoice entry on every nonempty input and returns an empty ranking for a single entry.
findings.failure_scenario: When entries contains one invoice, the loop executes zero times and returns [] instead of that invoice.
findings.title: Include the first invoice entry in the ranking

findings.body: The default list is created once and mutated by every call that omits events. Use a None default and initialize a fresh list inside the function.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events('created') followed by register_shipment_events('shipped') returns {'shipped': ['created', 'shipped']} on the second call, contaminating the new registration with the earlier event.
findings.title: Create a fresh default event list for each call

This violates the constant-time contract and adds O(n) work and memory even for already sorted input. Reuse the input list so the existing empty check and last-element access remain constant time.

findings.body: The viability condition depends only on whether the zone is nonempty and the weight is positive; it does not depend on the carrier. Multiply the number of nonempty zones by the number of positive weights once, then assign that count to each carrier, reducing O(C × Z × W) work to O(C + Z + W).

findings.body: Two lists and a manual membership loop are unnecessary for first-seen deduplication. Dictionaries preserve insertion order, so dict.fromkeys() expresses the entire operation directly and avoids repeatedly scanning the seen list.

    return dict.fromkeys(carriers, count)

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: The stated intent is a refactor, but this replaces an in-memory summary helper with database access and interpolates an owner identifier directly into executable SQL. This introduces a security-sensitive operation rather than preserving existing behavior. Move the loader into an explicitly scoped change and bind owner_id using the cursor driver's parameter API.
findings.failure_scenario: If an externally controlled owner_id contains `' OR '1'='1`, the interpolated WHERE clause matches other owners' orders, exposing rows beyond the requested owner.
findings.title: Separate the new SQL loader from the refactor and parameterize it

findings.body: Starting the loop at index 1 excludes entries[0] from the result regardless of its score. Ranking should reorder the supplied entries, not silently discard the first one.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-entry invoice list returns an empty ranking; a larger list always loses its first entry even when that entry has the highest score.
findings.title: Include the first invoice entry in the ranking

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default list is created once and mutated by events.append on every call that omits events. Independent calls therefore accumulate each other's shipment events. Use a None default and initialize a new list inside the function.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events("created") and then register_shipment_events("shipped") without explicit lists returns {"shipped": ["created", "shipped"]} on the second call, contaminating its event history with the first call.
findings.title: Create a fresh default event list for each call

findings.body: The condition hardcodes 5000 and ignores the threshold argument. Callers cannot control the review cutoff, producing both missed flags and unnecessary flags whenever their threshold differs from 5000.
findings.failure_scenario: With threshold=1000, a row whose total is 2000 is omitted even though it crosses the requested review threshold.
findings.title: Compare backorder totals against the supplied threshold

findings.anchor: """Load queued order rows for one owner through an open cursor."""
findings.body: The public contract says this loads queued orders, but the query filters only by customer_id and can return orders with any status. Remove the queued-only claim if all statuses are intended, or add the appropriate status predicate.
findings.suggestion: """Load order rows for one owner through an open cursor."""
findings.title: Align the loader docstring with its status filtering

findings.body: The documented chronological-order assumption means the newest record is already the last element. Sorting evaluates a key for every record and allocates a new list, requiring at least O(n) time and memory instead of the promised constant-time lookup. Reuse the input list with the existing empty-list check and final-element access.
findings.failure_scenario: When a large chronological queue is passed to retrieve its newest identifier, each lookup scans and copies the entire queue rather than accessing its last element, increasing latency and temporary memory use with queue size.
findings.title: Use the chronological input directly instead of sorting it

findings.body: `seen` is a list, so each membership check scans previously encountered labels. With mostly distinct labels, this performs O(n²) comparisons. Use a set for `seen` and replace `seen.append(label)` with `seen.add(label)`; keep the separate `labels` list to preserve first-seen order.
findings.failure_scenario: A large batch of distinct payment labels causes increasingly long membership scans, making deduplication quadratic instead of expected linear time.
findings.title: Use a set for payment-label membership checks

findings.body: The predicate depends only on whether a zone is nonempty and a weight is positive, not on the carrier or the pairing. Enumerating every combination for every carrier costs O(carriers × zones × weights). Count nonempty zones and positive weights separately, multiply those counts, and reuse the result for each carrier to reduce the work to O(carriers + zones + weights).
findings.failure_scenario: With 100 carriers, 1,000 zones, and 1,000 weights, the function performs 100 million predicate checks even though a few thousand input visits suffice, substantially increasing routing latency.
findings.title: Compute the viable combination count once without nested scans

findings.body: Neither validity condition depends on the carrier, and the zone and weight conditions are independent. Every carrier therefore receives the product of the two valid-input counts. The three nested loops needlessly enumerate combinations to obtain that same number. Replace the body after the docstring with two counts and a dictionary comprehension.

count = sum(bool(zone) for zone in zones) * sum(weight > 0 for weight in weights)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Count valid zones and weights once instead of enumerating combinations
